def: What an item was worth when it was damaged: replacement cost minus wear and age. Many policies pay ACV unless you have replacement cost cover.
A high-speed fan that blows air across wet floors and walls to speed up evaporation. Restoration crews place them in a pattern around the room.
A portable machine that pulls room air through a HEPA filter to catch mold spores and dust during cleanup.
A metal rod inside a tank water heater that corrodes in place of the tank. A worn-out rod lets the tank rust and leak.
link: Water heater leaking from the bottom

def: A cleaner that kills or slows bacteria and mold on surfaces after water damage.
A one-way valve on a home's sewer line that lets waste flow out but closes if sewage tries to flow back in.
Category 3 water: highly contaminated water such as sewage or floodwater from rivers. It needs protective gear and disinfection.
Clean water from a sanitary source, such as a broken supply line. It can turn into Category 2 or 3 if it sits.
Gray water that holds some contamination, such as washing machine or dishwasher discharge.
Black water that is grossly contaminated, such as sewage, toilet backflow with feces, or floodwater from outside.
A scale from Class 1 to 4 in the IICRC S500 standard. It rates how much of a room got wet and how much water soaked in. It sets how much drying gear a job needs.
Plastic sheeting and air pressure control that keep dust, mold or sewage inside the work area.
The shallow space under a home with a raised floor. It traps moisture and is a common place for hidden water damage.
The amount you pay on a claim before insurance pays. Many policies have a separate, higher deductible for wind, hail or hurricanes.
A machine that removes moisture from the air. Restoration crews use low-grain refrigerant (LGR) or desiccant units that dry air far more than household models.
A dehumidifier that pulls water from the air with a drying material instead of cold coils. It works well in cold spaces and dense materials.
The moisture reading of a dry, unaffected material in the same building. Drying is done when wet materials match it.
Gypsum board used for most walls and ceilings. It wicks water upward and often has to be cut out after a leak.
White, chalky mineral deposits left on concrete or brick when water passes through and evaporates. It is a sign of moisture.
A small tank on the water heater line that absorbs pressure as water heats. A failed one can make the relief valve drip.
link: Water heater leaking from the bottom

def: For insurance, flood means water covering normally dry land, such as a river rising or storm surge. Standard home policies leave it out.
An area FEMA maps for flood risk. High-risk zones start with A or V, and lenders require flood insurance there for federally backed mortgages.
A water line that has iced up. The pressure that builds between the ice and a closed faucet is what usually splits the pipe.
link: What to do when a pipe bursts

def: Category 2 water with some contamination, such as washer or dishwasher discharge or a toilet overflow with urine only.
A high-efficiency air filter. It traps at least 99.97% of particles 0.3 microns in size. Air scrubbers and HEPA vacuums use it.
The most common home insurance form. It covers the house against any risk that isn't excluded, and your things against listed risks.
Renters insurance. It covers the tenant's belongings and liability, not the building.
Condo insurance. It covers the inside of the unit, improvements and belongings, while the HOA's master policy covers the building.
The force of groundwater pushing against basement walls and floors. It drives water through cracks and joints.
A ridge of ice at the roof edge that traps melting snow. The water backs up under shingles and leaks into ceilings and walls.
The ANSI/IICRC standard for professional water damage restoration. It defines water categories, damage classes and drying practice.
A thermal camera that shows heat differences. Wet spots read cooler, so it helps find hidden water in walls.
A low-grain refrigerant dehumidifier. It can dry air to much lower humidity than a household unit, which speeds up structural drying.
The emergency steps that stop damage from getting worse: stopping the water, extraction, tear-out and drying.
A tool that measures how much water is in wood, drywall or concrete. Readings show where water spread and when drying is done.
A fungus that grows on damp materials. Indoor mold can start within 24 to 48 hours after water damage if materials stay wet.
The National Flood Insurance Program, run by FEMA. It sells flood policies through insurers and agents, usually with a 30-day wait.
The part of a home or renters policy that pays for your things, like furniture, clothes and electronics.
A valve where the water main enters the home that lowers street pressure. High pressure strains pipes, hoses and water heaters.
link: What to do when a pipe bursts

def: How much moisture the air holds, compared with the most it could hold. The EPA advises keeping it below 60%, ideally 30 to 50%.
Removing and cleaning up a hazard, such as mold or sewage, after the cause is fixed.
Insurance that pays to replace a damaged item with a new one of similar kind, without taking off for age.
The pipe that carries waste from a house to the city sewer main. In many cities the owner is responsible for it.
A leak in a water line under a concrete slab foundation. It can wet flooring for weeks before anyone notices.
Drying the building itself, such as framing, subfloor and concrete, with air movers, dehumidifiers and monitoring.
The plywood or board layer under finished flooring. It can trap water and swell after a leak.
Insurance wording for damage that happens fast and by surprise, like a burst pipe. Slow leaks and wear usually don't count.
A pump in a basement pit that sends groundwater away from the home before it rises over the floor.
The temperature and pressure relief valve on a water heater. It opens to release water if tank heat or pressure gets too high.
link: Water heater leaking from the bottom

def: Removing wet materials that can't be dried, such as soaked drywall, insulation and carpet pad, so the structure can dry.
An add-on (endorsement) to a home policy that pays for damage from water or sewage backing up through drains or a failed sump pump.
Removing standing water with pumps and extractors. It is the fastest way to cut drying time.
Stopping water damage from spreading: extraction, removing wet materials and drying, before repairs start.
How water climbs up porous materials like drywall and carpet pad, spreading damage above the waterline.
Estimating software many insurers and contractors use to price repair work line by line.
